meta.name: Structure Fire — 35% TBSA Burns with Airway Involvement

patient.name: Renee Castillo
patient.chiefComplaint: Burns and hoarse voice after being pulled from a house fire

history.hpi: Patient was asleep when a kitchen fire spread through her apartment. She was found by fire crews in a smoke-filled bedroom and carried out. She is coughing, her voice is progressively hoarser, and she has visible partial and full-thickness burns to her face, neck, and both forearms.
history.events: Structure fire in a first-floor apartment, patient trapped in a smoke-filled bedroom for an estimated 5-8 minutes before rescue

scene.dispatch: Structure fire, one patient rescued by fire crews, burns reported
scene.location: Front lawn of a two-story apartment building, patient triaged by fire crew after extraction
scene.safety: Fire controlled to unit of origin, scene cleared by fire command, no ongoing hazard to EMS crew
scene.bystanders: Fire crew who extracted the patient; neighbors gathered on the sidewalk
visualCues: Soot around the mouth and nose
Partial and full-thickness burns to face, neck, and bilateral forearms
Heavy smoke haze still visible from the building

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 39-year-old female just extracted from a smoke-filled apartment. She is alert, coughing, with soot around her mouth and nose, singed nasal hairs, a hoarsening voice, and visible burns to her face, neck, and forearms.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but hoarse voice, mild inspiratory stridor beginning
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, 26/min, occasional productive cough with dark-flecked sputum
otherFindings: Soot around mouth and nares, singed nasal hairs and eyebrows
Partial and full-thickness burns to face, neck, and bilateral forearms, estimated 35% TBSA
Voice progressively more hoarse over the last several minutes
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can't... stop coughing... my throat feels tight." (hoarse, breathy voice)

transitions.if: Early RSI performed for airway burn
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes stridor, worsening hoarseness, and singed nasal hairs as sentinel signs of a rapidly progressing airway burn and proceeds with early RSI before edema causes complete obstruction.
Crew prioritizes burn wound care and pain management over the deteriorating airway, delaying intubation while stridor and hoarseness worsen.

phases.name: Early RSI performed for airway burn
phases.description: Recognizing the sentinel signs of an airway burn, the crew performs early RSI before swelling progresses to complete obstruction.
phases.triggerCondition: Onset of stridor and a changing voice are sentinel signs of a potentially significant airway burn that can rapidly progress to obstruction, so the crew elects to secure the airway early rather than waiting for further deterioration.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Preoxygenating prior to RSI, stridor still present but airway not yet obstructed
otherFindings: Preoxygenated with high-flow oxygen and positive pressure for 2 minutes prior to RSI
Fentanyl, etomidate, and rocuronium administered in sequence
Successful first-pass intubation with 7.5 mm ETT

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize stridor and hoarse voice as sentinel signs of a significant airway burn
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Onset of stridor and change in voice are sentinel signs of potentially significant airway burns, which may rapidly lead to airway obstruction or respiratory failure.
expectedActions.rationale: These findings predict rapid progression to complete airway obstruction if not addressed early.

expectedActions.shortAction: Preoxygenate with high-flow O2 and positive pressure for 2 minutes before RSI
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient should be pre-oxygenated with high flow oxygen, and positive pressure ventilation for a minimum of two minutes prior to the procedure.
expectedActions.rationale: Adequate preoxygenation limits the risk of peri-intubation hypoxia.

expectedActions.shortAction: RSI: fentanyl 65 mcg IV (65 kg × 1 mcg/kg), etomidate 13 mg IV (65 kg × 0.2 mg/kg), rocuronium 65 mg IV (65 kg × 1 mg/kg)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Consider pre-medication with Fentanyl, 1 mcg/kg... Administer induction sedative agent: Etomidate IV push, 0.2-0.3 mg/kg... Administer paralytic agent: Rocuronium IV push, 1 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Weight-based induction and paralysis optimize first-pass intubation success.

expectedActions.shortAction: Intubate with 7.5 mm ETT (adult female sizing), confirm with waveform capnography
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Absent significant airway swelling or underlying anatomic abnormalities, initial tube size (internal diameter in millimeters) for adult females should be 7.5, adult males 8.0... Confirm placement of advanced airway... with waveform capnography (most reliable)
expectedActions.rationale: Waveform capnography is the most reliable confirmation of correct tube placement.

transitions.condition: With the airway secured, the crew estimates TBSA, initiates fluid resuscitation, and prepares the patient for burn center transport.

phases.name: Fluids and burn care initiated
phases.description: With the airway secured, the crew estimates TBSA, begins fluid resuscitation per the Rule of Ten, dresses the burns, and prepares for burn center transport.
phases.triggerCondition: After the airway is secured, the crew shifts focus to TBSA estimation, fluid resuscitation, wound coverage, and warming en route to a burn center.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, perfusing well
otherFindings: TBSA estimated at 40% (rounded) via Rule of Nines, second- and third-degree burns to face, neck, bilateral forearms
Burns covered with dry dressings, jewelry removed, blisters left intact

expectedActions.shortAction: Estimate TBSA at 40% (rounded) using Rule of Nines, excluding first-degree burns
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Estimate TBSA burned and depth of burn: Use "Rule of 9's"... First-degree/superficial burns (skin erythema only) are not included in TBSA calculations
expectedActions.rationale: Accurate TBSA estimation drives the fluid resuscitation rate.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate LR at 400 mL/hr (40% TBSA × 10; 65 kg patient, within the 40–80 kg bracket)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: For persons over 40 kg, the initial fluid rate can also be calculated using the "Rule of 10": Calculate the TBSA (round to nearest 10%). Multiply TBSA x 10 = initial fluid rate (mL/hr) {for persons between 40–80 kg}
expectedActions.rationale: Weight- and TBSA-based fluid resuscitation prevents burn shock while avoiding over-resuscitation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Remove jewelry and wet clothing, cover burns with dry dressing, leave blisters intact, no gels/ointments
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Remove wet clothing (if not stuck to the patient)... Remove jewelry... Leave blisters intact... Cover burns with dry dressing or clean sheet... Do not apply gels or ointments
expectedActions.rationale: Minimizes contamination and further tissue injury while avoiding materials that complicate burn center care.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply warming measures to prevent systemic heat loss
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Prevent systemic heat loss and keep the patient warm
expectedActions.rationale: Large TBSA burns impair thermoregulation and predispose to hypothermia.

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to burn/trauma center given airway involvement and TBSA > 10%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport to most appropriate trauma center when there is airway or respiratory involvement... Consider transport directly to burn center if partial or full thickness burns (TBSA) greater than 10%
expectedActions.rationale: Airway involvement and significant TBSA both mandate burn center-capable transport.

phases.name: Airway management delayed
phases.description: The crew focuses on burn wound care and pain control while the airway burn progresses, and stridor worsens toward complete obstruction.
phases.triggerCondition: Intubation is delayed while the crew manages visible burns and pain, allowing airway edema to progress toward complete obstruction.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Worsening stridor, near-complete obstruction, unable to speak
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Severe accessory muscle use, 32/min, minimal air movement audible
otherFindings: Stridor now audible without a stethoscope
Severe accessory muscle use and tracheal tug

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize impending complete obstruction; perform surgical airway when oxygenation/ventilation cannot be achieved
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: When patients cannot be oxygenated/ventilated effectively using the above interventions, or when conventional airway approaches are impossible, surgical airway management is a reasonable option if the clinician has competency in the procedure and risk of death for not escalating airway management seems to outweigh the risk of a procedural complication
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed recognition of a closing airway burn can progress to complete obstruction requiring a surgical airway.
